 Peter Everitt, father of Iowa punter Boston Everitt, didn't let the FAA ground stop deter him from seeing his son punt in Iowa City on Saturday. Scott Dochterman / The Athletic 
 By Scott Dochterman Nov. 14, 2026 Updated 4:38 pm EST Share article 25 IOWA CITY, Iowa — A real-life version of the movie “Planes, Trains and Automobiles” involved two hemispheres, a pair of flights, the world’s largest ocean, and a 6-foot-8 Aussie football legend crammed in the back of a car for 14 hours.
 All to watch his son’s college football game in person.
 It took 40 hours without sleep, but by Saturday morning, Peter Everitt, father of Iowa punter Boston Everitt, made it to his hotel room after a journey that only seemed to be missing a polka band .
 Advertisement
 The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights Friday afternoon, impacting more than a million passengers — including Iowa’s opponent, Purdue, which canceled its flight and instead rode buses for its 330-mile trek. Few of the cancellations made for fun stories, but Peter’s is probably the most interesting.
 “This is typical of him for something like that,” Peter’s wife, Sheree, said Saturday morning. “Trouble finds him.”

 Peter and Sheree have made multiple trips from Australia to Iowa since their son committed to the football program last winter. Sheree was already in Iowa City when Peter planned a quick weekend trip, which was supposed to last 36 hours before heading back home.
 After his shift as a popular morning radio host along Australia’s Gold Coast, Peter flew from Brisbane, Australia, to San Francisco, then Denver without incident. Then midafternoon on Friday, he joined thousands of others stranded on the tarmac.
 “The pilot goes, ‘We’ve all got to get off the plane,'” said Everitt, who is an Australian Rules Football Hall of Fame member. “Don’t ask questions because I know as much as you guys.”
 The 2 p.m. flight from Denver to Cedar Rapids, Iowa, turned into a 4 p.m. delay and later a 6 p.m. cancellation. Peter started looking at possible arrangements in case no flights made it out of Denver, while Sheree contacted people to help with travel contingencies.
 There was a train to Iowa, but the station was on the other side of Denver. Sheree reserved a rental car, but she worried about Peter making a 13-hour drive across the expansive interstate with little sleep. The other option was to stay in Denver and hope for a morning flight to Cedar Rapids.
 Before deciding, Sheree sent a note on social media asking if anyone was interested in “a nice night drive to Iowa City, look me up.” Within minutes, a person she had met at a previous tailgate reached out, saying some friends of friends knew two women who rented a car and were planning to drive to Iowa.
 Advertisement
 “I just ring (Peter), ‘You just need to get off at Hertz. There’s a lady in the car park,’” Sheree said. “He’s like, ‘Who?’ And I’m like, ‘I don’t know.’”
 Peter met Danielle Chickenn and Lacy Hawkins, two sisters from Burlington, Iowa, which is located about 70 miles southeast of Iowa City. Peter crammed in the back seat, and they started their journey east. They got lost for a bit and had to backtrack, stopped for salami, licorice and energy drinks at a gas station, and made it to Des Moines by 5 a.m., where Peter met another friend, who drove him the final 110 miles to Iowa City.
 “It was epic,” Peter said. “It was planes, trains, automobiles, a bus and two girls from Burlington in a tiny Hertz rental car.”
 Peter Everitt (center) hitched a ride from Denver to Des Moines, Iowa, overnight after his flight to Iowa was grounded. (Courtesy of Peter Everitt)
